# Space Atrapos - Pilot's guide

# basics | Getting started
Your first steps, the controls, and how this guide and the game's tooltips work.

## start | Welcome, pilot | keywords: Respawn, Load saved game, Main menu, CRT filter, attract mode
You fly a light fighter in **New Hellas**, a galaxy of 58 star systems - you start in its Atrapos sector, round Knossos - where six Greek star empires, the independents and the Sea Peoples raiders compete. Destroy raiders, collect what they drop, trade, take quests, and spend your drachmas on better ships, equipment and technology.

![](shot:space_hud)
- **Click** empty space to fly there; **click an enemy** (red) to attack it; fly over glowing **loot** to collect it.
- You start in orbit above **Amnissos** - its **land** button takes you down to walk around - near **Kephala Outpost**. Land on Amnissos first: **Kilon Alios**, the hooded wanderer by the landing pad, gives you the story. Click a station to dock: repair, trade, outfit, and pick up jobs (**Missions**). A **yellow targeting mark** - a hollow triangle pointing down - floats over whoever has a quest for you - Kilon until you take the story, stations while you have room for another mission.
- **Tab** opens the [Ship Computer](doc:computer); **M** the sector map; **G** the galaxy map; **Esc** the menu (save, load, settings) - and, with a window open (the Ship Computer, a map, a station, the Field Computer), Esc closes it first (at a station: undocks); **F1** this guide.
- **Continue**: the title screen's first button (shown once you have a save) loads your **latest save** - whichever slot, quicksave or autosave is newest; hover it to see which.
- **Talos**, the game's editor, opens from the title screen, from the **Esc menu** in a game, or with **F8** anywhere in space or on a planet: it opens over the game, which waits underneath, paused - leaving Talos (its **Back** button, Esc, or F8 again) puts you straight back where you were.
- **Settings** (Esc, or the title screen): the window, text sizes, the volumes, the controls, the CRT filter, the FPS counter - and the first steps of the game turning 3D: **Characters drawn from** - *3D model* (your automaton is its actual 3D model, drawn live: it turns smoothly to any direction and moves between the keyed frames), *Rendered sprites* (pictures rendered from the models: 30 frames a second, 8 views) or *Classic sprites* (the original hand-drawn two-pose pictures, kept as a backup) - and **3D terrain**: the planets' ground as real geometry (every tile a square at its height, cliffs and ramps solid, seen by a 3D camera) or, off, the 2D tiles as before. Both take effect at the next landing.
- **Saving**: **Esc > Save Game** shows **6 save slots** - each with when it was saved, where you were (the system, and the planet if you were on one), your ship and drachmas. Pick an empty slot, or save over one (click it twice: it asks first). **Load** (in the menu or on the title screen) shows the same list; the delete button (twice) erases a save. A save made **on a planet** loads back **down there, where you stood**. Loading shows a **loading screen** (which save, a bar, what's being done - restoring the galaxy, landing on the planet) until the game is ready to play. **F5 quicksaves** (its own Quicksave slot) and **F9 quickloads** it - anywhere, in space or on a planet (rebind them in Settings > Controls). The game also **autosaves** (its own Autosave slot) - every 5 minutes at first, never while you're under attack - and whenever you dock, arrive in a new system or land: **Settings > Game** chooses how often (off, or every 2, 5, 10, 15 or 30 minutes) and whether docking, jumps and landings autosave too. Both show at the top of the Load list.
If your ship is destroyed, **Respawn** puts you in a new ship at the nearest station with everything you've done kept - the story, your missions, reputation and drachmas - except your cargo, a tenth of your drachmas (the insurance) and **one thing you carried** - a random stack from your inventory, a system, or one of your fitted weapons (never a small Pulse Cannon or a story item). Whatever you lose dying - in space or on a planet - goes on a **lost list** that is kept in your save, however many times you die: every enemy you destroy or defeat yourself (a ship, a pirate, an animal) has a **10 % chance** to bring one of those things back, and **ITEM REGAINED** shows its name on screen for a few seconds. You can also **load** your latest save or go back to the **main menu**. The game never stops to load: its pictures stream in while you play (a faint shape stands in for one not loaded yet), and the console's **loading tab** shows it. The console (bottom left) has two tabs, picked by the icons at its top: the **event log** and the **loading console** - the loading tab's icon has a thin line under it showing the progress of the work under way, whichever tab you're on. The loading console's history (with a scroll bar, kept for the whole session - look back through it whenever you like) names each thing loaded or made: a picture, each piece of a solar system, a planet's plan, each chunk of its ground. Under it, the **memory pool**: how much the loaded assets take, of its room - twice what the game usually needs (every picture, and the surfaces of the system's planets). Then a bar shows how far the work under way is, and under that the **memory map**: the pool's room as a strip, each kind of asset (planet surfaces, monsters, buildings and tiles, ships, stations...) an area as wide as the memory it takes - hover over one for how many, how much, and its biggest assets with their size and priority. Nothing loaded is let go unless the room runs out; then the least used, by that priority (it rises each time something is used, and fades with time), that nothing on screen shows are unloaded, each named in the console in orange, and come back when they're needed. A **solar system streams in**: you fly from the first moment while its planets, moons, stations, gates, nebulae, ships, monsters and asteroid fields come in around you, nearest first, each fading in. Every landable planet's **surface is built ahead** in the background, one after another, nearest first (in a browser, the nearest three) - landing on any of them takes just the animation. Planets are made **chunk by chunk** (32 x 32 tiles): the ground round you first, then outward as you walk, a plain plate of the ground's colour where it isn't made yet. Leave the title screen alone for 30 seconds and the game plays itself - move the mouse or press anything to come back, on an old CRT screen. **Settings** comes in five tabs - **Display** (resolution, fullscreen, CRT filter, FPS counter), **Text** (text sizes - whatever you pick, no text is ever smaller than 12 px, and everything on a screen follows its size, even what appears after it opened), **Sound** (volumes), **Controls** (keys and gamepad) and **Game** (autosaves); **Q / E** or **LB / RB** switch tabs - and always fits the window, scrolling when its tab is too long. **Display** has an **FPS counter** switch (off at first - turn it on to see frames a second and the frame time at the top right, beside the minimap, green at 60 and above, over a live graph of each frame's time - lines at 600, 240 and 60 FPS), a **CRT filter** switch for that look all the time (off at first), and **Tune...** opens its own page: on in attract mode or not, and a slider for every part of it - curvature, round corners, scanline size and strength, phosphor mask, colour fringe, dark rim, brightness, flicker and the rolling band - previewed live while the page is open. See [Controls](doc:controls) for everything else.
- **The interface** is a ship's console in amber on smoked black glass: a button lights up solid amber under the mouse, the lit tab is the page you're on, and steel blue marks data, friendly things and your shields. (Talos's Library has a GUI room where the look can be changed, among them the older teal console.)
- **Sound**: space is full of it - your engine (louder as you speed up), each weapon's shot, hits on your shields and hull, explosions, the mining beam, loot, docking, landing and jumping; stations hum as you pass and jump gates shimmer. Music plays throughout - its own track on the title screen, in space and on planets, fading from one to the next. The story is **spoken**: each character's lines are read aloud in their own voice as they appear (Kilon's deep, faintly metallic voice, Ariadne, Daidalos, Asterion's low growl, the narrator, Kephala Outpost over the radio), stopping when you move on. **Settings > Sound** has the volumes: **Master** (everything), **Music**, **Sound effects** and **Voices** (0% turns one off).

## guide-tooltips | Tooltips and this guide
Buttons show icons: hover one for half a second to see its tooltip - its name, its keyboard shortcut in brackets and what it does.
- **Keep hovering for 12 seconds** and the tooltip **pins**: it stays when you move away and its links can be clicked. Close it with its blinking ✕, a right-click or a click outside it - or just open another tooltip.
- The links open this guide at the right page. **Back / Forward** (the arrows, Alt+Left / Alt+Right, or the mouse's side buttons) move through the pages you've read, like a web browser.
- **F1** opens the guide at the page for where you are (space, a station, the Ship Computer, a planet).

## archive | The Archive: every book in one place | keywords: Archive, Search every book, Pilot's Guide, Tutorial, Encyclopedia, Controls, Versions, Talos Manual
This guide is one of the books of the **Archive** - all of the game's documentation in one window. Its shelf: the **Pilot's Guide** (how everything works), the **Tutorial** (first steps, lesson by lesson), the **Encyclopedia** (ships, stations, gear, worlds and the lore of ancient Greece - only what you've discovered, each with its picture), **Controls** (every action and the keys and buttons bound to it now), **Versions** (what each version of the game brought, patch by patch) and the **Talos Manual** (the game's editor). **Search every book** finds the pages, in all of them, that have all your words. Links lead to any book's pages; **Back / Forward** retrace your steps. Open it with **F1** (at the page for where you are), a **Guide** button, the **Archive** tab of the Ship Computer or the Field Computer, or **Archive** in the Esc menu and on the title screen.

![](shot:archive)

## controls | Controls
- **Flying:** click empty space to fly there; hold and drag to steer. **E** docks at a nearby station.
- **Combat:** click an enemy to lock on and attack; Shift + right-click > Stop attacking. Click a **neutral** ship once to follow it (no firing) - click it again to attack it.
- **Zoom:** the mouse wheel zooms - in space, on planets and on every map; a click of the **middle button** puts the zoom back.
- **Scanner (right-click in space):** right-click an asteroid (within 1.6k) and a laser sweeps it - then it stays highlighted with its kind and the ore it holds. Right-click the **navigation beacon** beside the star to scan it (6 seconds, within 1.6k): you get the system's **navigation report** (see [Navigation reports](doc:nav-reports)). Right-click empty space for the **probe scanner** (if you have one - see [Probe scanner](doc:probes)): the system map opens with its PROBES panel. **Shift + right-click** opens the menu (stop attacking, hail, maps, Level Editor). **1-3** pick a weapon, **4-6** use systems (afterburner, shield booster, repair kit). **H** hails a ship.
- **Windows:** **Tab** Ship Computer · **M** sector map · **G** galaxy map · **T** trade routes on a map · **I** inventory · **Esc** closes the open window, else the menu · **F1** this guide.
- **In menus:** **W/A/S/D** or the arrows move between buttons (the first press picks the first one), **Enter** or **Space** presses it, **Q / E** switch tabs (in windows with tabs; **1-9** still jump to one).
- **Gamepad:** the **left stick** flies the ship (and walks you on planets; let go to stop), **RT** attacks the nearest enemy, **LB / RB** switch weapons in flight and tabs in menus, **Y** docks / undocks (Shift + D undocks on the keyboard), **Back** the Ship Computer, **Start** the menu, the **D-pad** (or the stick) moves through menus, **A** selects, **B** closes the Ship Computer and the maps.
- **Rebinding:** every key and gamepad button above can be changed in **Settings > Controls** (two keys and one gamepad input an action); right-click a binding to clear it, a red one is used twice. Saved at once.
- **On a phone or a tablet** (the web version, in a browser): a **tap** is a click - fly or walk there, hold to keep going, hold on a rock to cut it. **Two fingers tapped together** are the right button (scan a rock, open the probe scanner, the menu of things to do on foot), **pinch** to zoom, and buttons by the left edge stand in for the keys: **MENU**, **COMPUTER**, **MAP**, **ATTACK**, **DOCK** and **ZOOM + / -**. They step aside while a window is open (each has its own Close). The text starts a size up on a phone (Settings > Text). In a browser the page sets the window's size, so Settings has no Resolution, and the title screen no Exit.
- **On planets:** click to walk (hold to keep walking); click citizens to talk; click stairs to climb; click an enemy (or press **F**) to attack it; **1-9** use the toolbar's slots - the rifle, medicine, and your [skills](doc:skills): martial arts, the leap, spells (aimed where the mouse points); **K** the Spell Book; **M** or **Tab** the planet map; click your ship to take off.

# space-ch | In space
Flying, fighting, mining, the people you meet out there, and landing on planets.

## spaces | Local, planet, solar and galaxy space | keywords: Local space, Planet space, Solar space, Galaxy space
Space comes in four kinds:
- **Solar space** - a star system: its star, planets and moons, stations, gates, asteroid fields and the ships about their business. Where you fly most of the time.
- **Local space** - a pocket of space of its own, apart from the system round it: a **signal source** you drop into, or a ringed planet's **ring**. Its beacon sits in solar space; **ENTER** takes you in, **Leave** (or flying far out) brings you back beside it.
- **Planet space** - a planet's or moon's surface, where you land and walk as the automaton.
- **Galaxy space** - the galaxy of star systems and gate lanes, reached only through the **galaxy map** (G): plot a route there and jump system to system through the gates.

## space3d | Space Atrapos 3D | keywords: 3D: Continue, 3D: New game, Back to the title screen, Save game, Hyperion drive, gravity well, virtual stick, Market, Outfitting, Missions, Repair Bay, Ship's Log
The game in **3D**: star systems of the galaxy built in 3D, flown from **behind your ship**; planets of real procedural ground you fly down to, land on and walk; their plants and animals; pirates; stations to dock at. On the title screen, **3D: Continue** carries on **your latest save** (the galaxy, your credits and cargo, the system you're in) and **3D: New game** starts afresh. The 3D game saves into the **Autosave** slot - when you dock, when you come through a gate, at a station's Ship's Log, from the Esc menu (**Save game**) - in the same format as the 2D game, which loads it too.

![](shot:space3d)
- **Steering** - the mouse is a **virtual stick**: move it away from the middle (the ring on screen) and the ship pitches and turns, faster the further out; **C** (or the middle button) centres it. **A / D** roll. **W / S** set the throttle (it stays where you leave it; **X** stops), **Shift** boosts. A gamepad works too: the left stick steers, the triggers set the throttle.
- **The Hyperion drive** - **J**: after a two-second charge the ship races across the system at up to 250 km/s - any planet in seconds. Target a planet, station or gate first (**T**) and the drive takes you there: it turns the nose to it while you leave the mouse alone (it engages once you're lined up), steers round anything in the way, slows by itself as you arrive and drops you out about 1.5 km from it. **Gravity** holds it back: every planet, moon and the star has a **gravity well** (a dozen times its radius) - the deeper in, the slower the drive (the panel names the well). Coming too close to anything, or being shot, drops you out.
- **Planets are real ground** - every planet and moon is a whole world of procedural terrain: continents and seas, mountain ranges, craters, ice caps, lava. What you see from orbit is the ground you fly down to: it grows finer as you come closer, down to a metre underfoot. Gas giants have no ground, only cloud bands.
- **Landing** - low (within 160 m) and slow (under 80 m/s) over dry, level enough ground, **L** sets the ship down. **E** gets out; beside the ship, **E** boards it; **L** or **Space** takes off.

![](shot:space3d_ground)
- **On foot** - **W A S D** walk where the camera looks, **Shift** runs, **Space** jumps, the mouse looks round. Shallows are waded, deep water swum. Each world has its own **plants** (trees, bushes, grass, flowers, crystals, fungi, cacti - from its seed and type) and **animals**: grazers that run from you, skittish runners, **predators** that hunt you - the biggest of them the world's **monsters**. The **left button** fires your rifle; the sights show what they're on. Out of health, your ship's drones bring you back beside it.
- **Pirate camps** - a red light on a mast: their guards, pirate androids, open fire when you come near.

![](shot:space3d_foot)
- **Markers** show the star, planets, stations, gates and ships near you; **T** targets what's nearest the middle of the view (its distance and time to arrive on the panel).
- **Ships and combat** - traders ply between the stations, the system's **patrols** circle them, and now and then **pirate raiders** come for you (more in lawless systems). The **left button** fires your twin lasers; with a ship targeted, the ring shows where to aim to hit it. **Shields** soak hits and come back; the **hull** doesn't (the Repair Bay fixes it). A raider destroyed pays its **bounty**. Lose your ship and you're back by the first station, repaired.

![](shot:space3d_fight)
- **Docking** - near a station, **F**: traffic control flies you in, under the station and up into its bay, to the **hangar**. Get out and walk it: the crew at their work, and **terminals** along the back wall (**E** beside one) - the **Market** (the station's real market: its stock and prices move as you trade), the **Repair Bay**, **Outfitting** (your 3D ship's upgrades: laser coils, shield capacitors, hull plating, engine tuning), **Missions** (bounty contracts on the system's raiders) and the **Ship's Log** (save). **L** or **Space** aboard undocks.
- **Gates** - fly through a gate's ring to jump to the system it leads to.
- **Camera** - the **wheel** moves it in and out; hold the **right button** to look round the ship. **H** hides the controls, **Esc** opens the menu.

![](shot:space3d_hangar)

## space | Flying and fighting | keywords: Land on, land
- **Moving** - click empty space: the ship turns and flies there, slowing as it arrives. Hold and drag to steer continuously.

![](shot:space_combat)
- **Attacking** - click an enemy to lock on (red brackets). Out of range, your ship closes in automatically and fires on its own. Keep clicking space to manoeuvre while firing.
- **Shields** (blue) absorb damage first and recharge a few seconds after the last hit. **Hull** (red) mends itself slowly out of a fight (faster with tech) and is repaired at stations or with repair kits. Both burn **fuel** as they come back: 2 for a full 100 points of shields, 5 for 100 points of hull - out of fuel, neither recharges.
- **Weapons and systems** are on the toolbar at the bottom: **9 slots** (keys **1-9**) you fill yourself - at first Pulse Cannon, Plasma Cannon, Missiles, Afterburner, Shield Booster and Repair Kit (1-6), three empty. **Every weapon fitted fires at your target together**, each on its own and from its own hardpoint on the hull; a weapon's key switches **all of that kind on or off** (lit while on) - hold your missiles for later, or the beam while you mine. **LB / RB** step through all weapons on, then each kind on its own. In the Ship Computer's inventory (**I**), **drag** a weapon, a system or repair kits onto a toolbar slot (or hover it and press **1-9**); **drag** a toolbar slot onto another to swap them - on the toolbar at the bottom too; right-click a slot to empty it. **Inventory slots** can be dragged too: drag a stack to another slot to arrange your hold (where you put things stays put). Locked slots must be bought at a station.
- **Cargo hold** - counted in **slots**, up to **100** of an item in each (250 iron ore take 3 slots); how many slots depends on your ship's class - from 12 on the smallest to 120 on a freighter (the starter ship has 16); Cargo Racks add more.
- **Loot** drops from destroyed ships and drifts towards you when you fly close; it vanishes after a minute.
- **Neutral ships** (green) never attack first; **Sea Peoples raiders** prey on everyone. Every raider you destroy outside a pirate system earns a **bounty** from the system's owner - about 135 dr for an interceptor, 160 for a fighter, 250 for a gunship, 360 for a frigate (x1.6 during Pirate Raids, +10 % when you're Friendly with the system's owner, +25 % when Allied) - on top of what its wreck drops.
- **Planets** with a **land** button over them can be visited - see [Planets](doc:planets).
- **Fuel** (the amber ring round the gauge): every **jump through a gate burns 10**, flying burns a trickle (more with the afterburner, which also takes 2 a burst), and so do your **shields recharging and your hull mending itself** (0.02 a shield point, 0.05 a hull point). With less than 10 you can't jump; with an empty tank only the emergency thrusters work (a third of your speed). **Refuel** at any station (the Repair tab: fill up at its fuel price, or pump in the fuel you carry in the hold - each unit fills 10), click fuel in your hold (the Ship Computer's inventory) to pump a unit in anywhere, or fit a **Star Energizer** and switch it on near the sun (within about 1,800 of its surface): it drains the star's power into your tank, 6 a second, a beam from the star to your ship. The tank's size goes by the hull class (the starter ship's: 100); **Fuel Tanks** add to it.
- **Electro** - a lightning weapon: the bolt strikes at once and leaps on to up to three more hostile ships nearby, each hit three quarters of the last, **electric** damage - and each ship it hits may be **stunned** for a moment (its drive dead, its guns silent). Some warships and raiders carry one too: their lightning can stun you (a **Faraday Mesh** resists it).
- **Shields and hull** - most hits do the same damage to shields and hull (the **Pulse Cannon**, your starting weapon, the Plasma Cannon, missiles). The **Beam Emitter** is different: a continuous blue beam while your target is in reach, it drains **shields twice as fast** as its damage but does only **a third to a hull** - strip their shields with it, then switch to something else (1-9) for the hull.
- **Projection Array** - a module (nose; a toolbar system, 25 s to recharge): it projects **two illusions** of your ship that fly in formation beside you - the same hull, heading and engine trail. Enemies can't tell which is real: each one attacking you (or turning on you while they're up) picks one of the three at random. An illusion **vanishes the moment it's hit**. Every 4 seconds your ship **swaps places** with one of them (a flash on all three hides it), so even watching where you went won't do. They last 15 seconds.
- **Cloak** - a module (hull; a toolbar system): switch it on and a shimmer sweeps over your ship until it's a clear lens on the stars behind it, only its edges catching the light - and **no enemy can see it** - ships hunting you lose you - as long as you **don't fire a weapon** (firing, or switching it off, ends it). Your **shields are down** while you're cloaked; when the cloak ends they come back to where they were over **2 seconds**.
- **Bouncer Plasma** - a ball of plasma that flies at your target and **bounces** on to the next enemy (ships it hasn't hit yet first), up to **6 hits**, each one full heat damage; then it bursts into a **web** that ties every ship it hit together for 6 seconds: slowed to under half their speed and unable to pull away from one another (glowing strands, the web's reach a faint ring). Some raiders and warships carry one too (gunships and frigates most often): their ball **webs you to them** - the ship that fired it and up to two of its wingmen - slowing you and holding you within reach of them until the web fades.
- **Wrecks** - destroyed ships and stations leave their **wrecks** behind: the hull greyed out, scorched and torn open, drifting slowly (they're gone after a few minutes; a station's stays much longer). With a **Salvage Rig** fitted, click a wreck: your ship flies up and cuts it apart - hold close for a few seconds (a station's takes ten) - for scrap, electronics, machinery, fuel, **spare parts** for the Repair Bay (always a few - more from a bigger ship, a handful from a station), now and then a piece of gear or **one of its weapons**, and from a ship that carried an **Electro** often the Electro itself (an Electro S: fitted to a free hardpoint that takes it, else into your hold).

![](shot:salvage)


## damage | Damage, afflictions and accuracy | keywords: Afflictions, Self-repair frozen, Accuracy, Evasion, Critical, Miss
**Your health gauge** (top left) - your ship's outline, filled with red liquid as high as its **hull** is, inside a ring filled with blue liquid as high as its **shields** are, and round that a ring of amber liquid as high as your **fuel** is (its rim turns red when there isn't enough left for a jump) - no panel, no numbers: hover the rings for them (on foot the same gauge shows the automaton's health and shield). Your drachmas show at stations and in the inventory.

**Afflictions** - when hits get through to your hull (or your automaton's body on foot) they damage its **parts** (see [the Repair Bay](doc:repair-bay)), and every damaged part is an **affliction**: an icon round your health gauge, clockwise from the top (your ship's in space, the automaton's on foot) - hover it for what it does and what's wrong in it. The **first** is always the same: **self-repair frozen** - while anything is damaged, the hull stops mending itself (out of a fight it otherwise creeps back by itself) and the automaton stops healing. The worse you're hurt the more pile up: below 80% of your hull at least one damaged part, below 60% two, then three, four, and five or more near the end. They go when the parts are repaired - by hand in the Repair Bay, or by a station's technicians.

**Near death** the whole window starts failing like a broken monitor: static, rolling bands, a flicker, cracks across the glass - more as it gets worse, never so much you can't see. Damaged ships (yours and others) crackle with **electrical faults**: arcs and sparks off the hull; your automaton too.

**Accuracy** - no shot is certain. Every shooter has an accuracy: your ship's (86% at a still target nearby; upgrades, sensors), every other ship's by its class, your automaton's (88%), pirates' and beasts'. Less against a target moving across your line of fire, a small fast one (its **evasion**), and further away. A **miss** is aimed past the target - you see the bolt fly by beside it - and does nothing (beams slide off for a moment, an Electro fizzles). **Critical hits**: now and then a shot strikes a weak spot for 1.6 times the damage ("CRITICAL"); upgrades raise the chance and the damage.

![](shot:damage)

## mining | Mining
Mining is done by hand, a vein at a time:

- **Prospect it**: right-click an asteroid (within 1.6k) and your scanner sweeps it. Then you know what it's **made of** - a mix of minerals, each rock its own (an **iron** rock: iron with copper, tin, sulphur and cobalt; **titanium**: with cobalt, silver, obsidian, orichalcum; **platinum**: with gold, silver, orichalcum, cobalt; the rings' **ice**: with sulphur, salt and obsidian) - and where its **veins** run: 2 to 5 glowing seams, each of one mineral and so much ore. The log lists them; the **mining readout** above the toolbar shows the mix.
- **Cut a vein**: click the rock to target it (you fly into range), then **hold the button on it** to fire the laser; let go to stop. Press near a vein to pick it (it's ringed); otherwise the nearest. The laser **heats** the vein - the readout's bar: below its band it cuts slowly or not at all; in the **green band** it cuts at full speed and builds **resonance** (the longer you hold it there the faster, up to x1.6); above it, it strains; at the top the vein **fractures** - a quarter of what's left breaks off as worthless rubble and the heat drops. So pulse it: hold, let go as it nears the top, hold again. Harder minerals (platinum, orichalcum, cobalt) heat faster.
- **Fragments**: what you cut floats to your ship as **fragments** of the mineral - sold as they are they fetch little; an on-board **refinery** turns each into a unit of the mineral (see [Industry](doc:industry)). An unprospected rock gives only **rubble**.
- The rock shrinks as it's mined and shatters when its veins are spent; a full **cargo hold** stops the laser. The sensors' **ore yield** and the weapon mounts' **mining speed** upgrades help.

![](shot:mining)

**Planetary rings** - a ringed planet's ring is a **local space** of its own: fly to the beacon on the ring and **ENTER**. Along a great curving band lie ice asteroids beyond counting - **ring ice** to cut and sell - and the miners of the system's empire (or independents) work them. Raiders come for the miners every minute or so: every raider you destroy while the miners are at work earns their empire's thanks (+1.5 reputation, on top of the bounty). A ring never runs out of rocks: leave when you like.

## signals | Signal sources | keywords: Enter, Leave, Signal source, Distress call, Combat signal, Debris field, Unknown bio-signature, Anomalous readings, Anomaly field
Every star system hides **signal sources** - 12 to 36 at a time (every kind among them), a fresh set every 20 minutes. The **probe scanner** finds them (see [Probe scanner](doc:probes)): pinned down to 100%, a signal is **located** and its **beacon** appears - in space, on your radar (diamonds) and on the system map. Click **ENTER** over a beacon to drop into it (from far away your ship flies there first): a **local space** of its own - no star, planets or stations - where something is going on. The panel at the bottom says what; **Leave** (or fly far out) takes you back beside the beacon. Finish one and it's gone; leave one unfinished and its beacon waits.

![](shot:signal_site)
- **Distress call** - a ship out of fuel. Fly up to it and transfer **5 fuel** (or rig its drive with **2 energy cells**) for drachmas and its empire's thanks. Sometimes it's bait.
- **Combat signal** - a freighter under attack by pirates. Kill them all while it lives and it pays you.
- **Debris field** - a wreck with its cargo drifting round it (it doesn't expire). Scavengers may come for it too.
- **Unknown bio-signature** - a creature: **Skylla**, a sea witch crowned in gold, rising from eight great writhing tentacles. She draws back her clawed hands, her eyes blaze, energy gathers at her snarling mouth and she fills space with bullet-hell patterns of glowing orbs - rings, spirals, aimed fans, curving blooms; hard to dodge, never impossible. Dead, she leaves alien alloy, data cores and drachmas. Or **Cerberus**, the three-headed hound in gold armour: every head breathes fire, the patterns coming from all three jaws in turn. Or **Cetus**, the sea monster Poseidon sent against Andromeda: it swims where it heads, raises rings of breaking waves - and dives into the void, its shadow sliding toward you, to breach where you were (get out of the ring). Or **Echidna**, the mother of monsters, half woman and half serpent: she rears up to loose her brood of serpents after you, closes a coil of them round you (find the gap), and spits venom that burns where it lands. Or **the Hydra** of Lerna, eight heads on one knot of coils, every one spitting from its own jaws: it bites with whichever head is nearest you, rears up to breathe rings of poison - and cut off one of its heads (every twelfth of its hull you take) and two grow in its place: a double head that keeps round the Hydra and fires at you too (up to twelve at once; kill them, or kill the Hydra and they die with it). Or **the Chimera** - lion, goat and serpent in one beast, each head fighting its own way: the lion roars rings of fire and breathes a cone of flame that sweeps across (the arc shows where it will go), the goat sprays embers and charges with lowered horns, the serpent spits venom that curves in on you - and rearing up, all three fire at once. Or **Charybdis**, the whirlpool that swallows the sea: a ring of teeth round a turning vortex, tentacles writhing at its rim. It spins out arms of waves and draws bubbles in from all round you - then it churns and drags everything toward its maw (fly away at full speed to break free; get pulled in and it bites), and swells to spew the swallowed sea back out. Each has its own bullets and patterns, changing as the fight goes on. Whichever it is, it dies hard - shaking and bursting before it blows apart - and its loot drops after the explosion.
  - **They hunt you.** Once a creature has seen you it never gives up the chase, and it is as fast as your ship. Leave its signal while it lives and a few seconds later it comes out of the void after you, into the system - as hurt as you left it - attacking any ship in its way. Kill it there for its loot; go back into its signal and it's waiting for you there; jump to another system and you've lost it (its beacon stays).
- **Anomalous readings** - a space anomaly with four nodes. Fly close to each and right-click it to scan; all four give **Anomaly Research Data** (research stations pay well). Its core burns.
- **Hazard: anomaly field** - a field of unstable anomalies that drain your shields and then burn your hull. Find the gaps and reach the **exit** for the cache there; fly out of its sides and you leave with nothing.

## probes | Probe scanner | keywords: Probes, Launch probes, Analyze, Recall probes, Signatures, Probe Scanner
The **Probe Scanner** (equipment; outfitters' SYSTEMS) finds what's hidden in a system - **anomalies** (signal sources), **ships** (hostile and neutral), **planets, moons and the star**, and **structures** (stations, gates, the navigation beacon). Right-click empty space (or the map's **PROBES** button) and the system map opens with its panel:

- **Launch** five probes where the map is centred - one in the middle, four round it - at the **reach** shown (1k to 32k: - / +). On the map each shows as a circle of its reach. **Drag** a probe to move it; the **wheel** over one changes its reach. **Move them as a group**: drag the gold **handle** above them (or **Shift + drag** any probe) and they all move together, keeping their formation; the **wheel over the handle** spreads them out or draws them in round their middle, and **Shift + wheel** over a probe changes every probe's reach at once.
- **ANALYZE** (3.5 s once they're in place): every signature within the probes' reach gets a **strength**. A probe covering it adds more the nearer it is to the probe's middle and the **tighter** the probe's reach; several probes together add up. Faint kinds (anomalies) need more than plain ones (a planet), and the sensors' **probe strength** upgrade raises them all.
- What it shows: under 25% an **unknown signature** somewhere in a wide circle; 25-75% its **kind**, in a smaller circle; 75-100% what it is, in a small one; **100%: located** - named, exactly placed, and (an anomaly) its **beacon** appears. Click a found one in the list to centre the map on it (a located one: set a course to it). So: sweep wide to see that something's there, then draw the probes in tight round it and analyze again.

![](shot:probes)

## comms | Comms
Press **H** (or Shift + right-click > Hail) to call your target or the nearest ship: traders share tips, patrols report on the war, raiders demand tribute. Station dockmasters and mission givers greet you in person. Conversations: **Continue** (Space, Enter or a click) shows the next line, **Skip** ends it.

# stations-ch | Stations
Everything you can do while docked.

## stations | Docking | keywords: Undock
Each system's main station bears its name (Zakros Archive, Sparta Barracks); the others are named after the empire's heroes, people, landmarks and cities - Pericles Lyceum, Menelaos Citadel, Sappho Observatory, Perseus Tholos. Click a station to fly there and dock, or press **E** close by. Docking pauses the game and recharges your shields for free; the station's **safe zone** (dashed ring) keeps enemies away. The tabs (keys **1-9**) are explained on the next pages; **Undock** (**Shift + D**, or pad Y) returns you to space.

## repair | Repair | keywords: Repair, Request an evaluation, Repair everything, Repair the part, Upgrade, Refuel, Pump
The **REPAIR** tab has three pages:

- **SERVICE** - the station's technicians. **Request an evaluation** (free) and they go over your ship and your automaton and list everything damaged: the **hull**, then each damaged part - its affliction - and the faults in it (even those you haven't traced), each with how long it takes, what it would cost you to do it yourself, and their price. Then repair **one thing**, **a part** (all its faults: its affliction goes) or **everything**. It isn't quick and it isn't cheap: up to **a minute** (the more there is, the longer - a bar shows the work, item by item), and at least **ten times** what the same repair costs you in materials and spare parts in the [Repair Bay](doc:repair-bay). Undock mid-repair and what isn't done yet is paid back.
- **UPGRADES** - every part of your ship and your automaton carries **stats** you can raise, five levels each, dearer each level: some fifty of them - hull and shields, armour and every resistance, shield recharge and its delay, the hull's self-repair, speed, handling, **evasion**, weapon damage, rate of fire, range, **accuracy**, **critical chance** and **critical damage**, system cooldowns, fuel tank and fuel efficiency, hold space, probe strength, ore yield, mining and refinery speed; the automaton's health, healing, damage, rate of fire, reach, accuracy, walking speed, evasion, armour and resistances. Pick the ship or the automaton, then a part. An upgrade lives in its part: while the part is damaged it gives only as much as the part still works. **Upgrade Kits** made on board fit them too (see [Industry](doc:industry)).
![](shot:station_service)

- **FUEL**: **Refuel** fills your tank at this station's fuel price (a tenth of its market price for a unit of fuel, per unit of tank); **Pump fuel from the hold** empties the fuel you carry into the tank (10 a unit).

## market | Market | keywords: Buy 1, Buy 10, Sell 1, Sell all, Trade routes
Every station has a live **commodities market**. New Hellas trades in **140 goods** in ten categories of fourteen - **Food & drink** (grain, olive oil, wine, honey, garum, saffron...), **Medicine** (dittany of Crete, nanomeds, Asklepian salve...), **Machinery**, **Technology** (processors, star reckoners, automaton brains...), **Energy** (deuterium, Greek fire, antimatter pods...), **Minerals** (copper, tin, silver, orichalcum, Parian marble...), **Luxuries** (silk, Tyrian purple, amber, red-figure vases, lyres...), **Arms**, **Wares & salvage** and **Exotics** (hydra scales, cyclops lenses, ambrosia...). A station deals in the original goods and in what its economy **produces** (cheap here, marked MADE HERE) and **uses** (dear here) - a research station in different goods from a mining colony, so hauling between them pays; a station also buys whatever you bring it. A **tab per category** (with how many of its goods this station trades) shows that category's goods - **Sell** (what the station pays you), **Buy** (what it asks; "-" when it has none), the **galactic average** price with how far this station's price is from it (green ▲: it pays more than average - a good place to sell; red ▼: less), **Supply** (bars and the station's stock) and **Demand** (bars: how badly the station needs it - only goods it uses), and what you carry. Click a good (or **W/S**, the arrows, the D-pad) to see it on the right: its prices, a quantity (**A/D**, or − / + / MAX; Shift + A or Shift + the arrows: by 10), **Buy** (Enter / pad A) and **Sell** (Backspace / pad X), and the **best prices within two jumps** - with the profit a unit over today's price here, and a button to plot a route there. Prices follow supply, and your own trades move them too: every unit you buy pushes the price up, every unit you sell pushes it down (harder where the good is scarce), and the push fades over a few minutes - so a full hold usually pays best sold across several stations. System states (boom, famine, war...) move prices. Most of what a station uses is shipped in by the NPC traders (and you); a station short of its inputs slows down and uses less.

![](shot:station_market)
- **Trade routes** (only what you know: a run starts at a station whose market you know - you've docked there - and ends at one you've found, come within sensor range of; be **Friendly** with an empire and it shares all of its markets): the sector map (M) and the galaxy map (G) have a trade layer (the cart button, or **T**): green arrows for the best runs - buy a good at one station, sell it at another - labelled with the good and the profit a unit. See their pages.

## outfitting | Outfitting | keywords: Fit, Remove, Buy Missiles, Buy Repair
- **Tabs**: Your ship (fitted modules and ship gear in your hold) · Weapons · Systems · Ship modules · Automaton gear · Supplies. Click a card to see it on the right: a large picture of it, its price and buttons, what it is, a weapon's or system's own stats, and **before → after** - every stat it would change (green better, red worse), worked out with your ship's (or automaton's) real numbers.

![](shot:station_outfitting)
- **Weapons come in sizes** - **XS, S, M, L, XL, XXL** - and go on the ship's **hardpoints**, each of a size too: two XS on an interceptor, three on the Atrapos (one S, two XS), four on a gunship (two M, two S), ten on a frigate, 14 on a cruiser, 18 on a battleship and **24 on a dreadnought** (two XXL). A weapon fits a hardpoint **its size or bigger**. Each size up hits 1.7 times harder, reaches a little further and fires a little slower - and costs 2.6 times as much. Not every kind comes in every size: Pulse Cannons XS-XL, Plasma Cannons and Missiles XS-XXL, the Beam Emitter S-XXL, the Electro and the Bouncer Plasma S-XL. A weapon is an item like any other: bought at an outfitter (the **WEAPONS** tab, a size at a time - it goes on a free hardpoint that takes it, else into your hold), salvaged from wrecks, sold; in the hold, click it (or drag it onto a free hardpoint on the equipment screen) to fit it; right-click a fitted one to take it out.

![](shot:station_weapons)

- Every fitting has its **area** of the ship: **weapons** on its **hardpoints** (the wings), weapon modifiers and sensors in the **nose**, armour, shields and repair systems in the **hull**, the drive's modules (Enhanced Thrusters, Afterburner, Star Energizer) at the **thrusters**, cargo racks, fuel tanks and the Salvage Rig in the **cargo bay**. How many each area takes depends on the hull class. The Ship Computer's inventory shows them as an **equipment screen**: your ship drawn large with each area's slots beside it - drag ship gear from the hold onto a free slot of its area.
- **Modules** come in ratings **E** (cheap) to **A** (best): shield generators, hull reinforcement, cargo racks, thrusters, shield cell banks...
- **Remove** sells a fitted item back for 80% of its price; **hold** takes a fitted module out into your hold instead (it's gear - see Gear). **Supplies** (missiles, repair kits) don't use cargo space.

## gear | Gear: equipment for your ship and your automaton | keywords: Quality, Loadout, Ship gear, Weapon mod, Armour, Core, Passive, resistance


**Gear** is equipment you fit to your **ship** or equip on your **automaton** (you on foot). Every piece comes in a **quality** from **E** (common) through D, C and B to **A** (masterwork): the better, the stronger - and the dearer. Gear is an item like any other: it sits in your hold or in what you carry, stacks, and can be sold.

- **Where it comes from** - the **Outfitting** tab of every station (pick a quality at the top, then buy: ship gear is fitted at once if a slot is free, else it goes into your hold; automaton gear goes into your hold); **destroyed ships** sometimes drop it (bosses always, tougher ships better); on planets **pirates**, **big beasts** and **containers** (chests, lockers - vaults most often); and every **signal source** you complete rewards a piece (better the harder the signal, two from an insane one).
- **Ship gear** fits the ship's **internal** and **utility** slots (how many depends on its class): stat modules (shields, hull, thrusters, cargo racks), **weapon modifiers** (Focusing Lens: damage; Capacitor Bank: fire rate; Targeting Computer: range - for every weapon), **plating** (resistances) and **passives** (Nanite Repair mends the hull). Fit it from the hold in the Ship Computer's inventory (click it, or drag it onto the Ship Gear row); right-click a fitted module to take it out. Weapons themselves go on the hardpoints (above).
- **The automaton's loadout** - its **equipment screen** shows the automaton with a slot at each part of it: the **weapon** in the right arm, a weapon mod in the right hand and one on the left arm, **armour** on the torso, the **core** in the head, the passives in the legs and on the back - 7 slots: a **weapon** (Laser Rifle, Pulse Carbine, Plasma Rifle, Rail Rifle, Cryo Rifle - each its own damage, rate, reach and damage type), two **weapon mods** (scope, amplifier, capacitor, stabiliser), **armour** (health and resistances), a **core** (healing, speed, longer overcharges) and two **passives**. Equip from the Ship Computer's inventory (gear in your hold) or the Field Computer's (gear you carry): click a piece, or drag it onto a slot; to take it off, **click the slot** (or drag it back onto your items, or right-click it) - it goes back where it came from, if there's room. Your stats change at once.
- **Damage types and resistances** - every hit is **energy** (pulse cannons, lasers, bolts, beams), **kinetic** (slugs, bites, rams), **explosive** (missiles), **heat** (plasma, fire breath, the volcanic beasts) or **cold** (frost). Resistance to a type takes that share off its hits (at most 75%). **Heat resistance** also eases Akrotiri's heat (your healing slows less), **cold resistance** the ice moons' footing (you're slowed less).

## shipyard | Shipyard | keywords: Buy the
Each station sells its empire's designs (and the independents'), a **tab per class** - interceptors, fighters, couriers, explorers, gunships, freighters, frigates, and the **capital ships**: cruisers, battleships and dreadnoughts - cheapest first, each with its hull, shields, speed, hold and hardpoints beside how they compare with your ship's. Within a class the dearer designs are the better ones; prices run from about 15,000 dr for an interceptor to millions for the great frigates - and far more for a capital ship. Every empire builds its own capital ships (for now drawn with its biggest hulls, larger), and a **war fleet** of six or more flies under one: a cruiser, a battleship from nine ships, a dreadnought leading a full twelve. Other ships carry weapons for their class too, firing from all over their hulls, and a salvaged wreck may give one of them up. Your current ship is traded in for 80% of what you paid for it (the fighter you start with counts as 2,500 dr, so it trades in for 2,000): you pay the difference. Cargo is kept; weapons go on the new ship's hardpoints that take them (the rest into your hold), and other fittings that don't fit it are sold back.

![](shot:station_shipyard)

## designer | Designer | keywords: Skin, Apply paint, Factory paint
Repaint your ship with the hue, saturation, brightness and tint sliders, or pick a ready-made **skin** (a colour swatch with its price, ✓ when owned). **Apply paint** pays and paints; **Factory paint** restores the original colours for free.

## sell | Selling cargo | keywords: Sell all cargo
Sell your loot and trade goods at this station's prices, one at a time, all of one kind, or **all cargo** at once (missiles, repair kits and story items are kept).

## empire | Empires, independents and your reputation | keywords: Reputation, Independent, Independents, outpost, forward base, Hostile, Unfriendly, Cordial, Friendly, Allied
You answer to no empire: what counts is your **reputation** with each of them - and with the **Independents** - from -100 to 100, in tiers: **Hostile** (below -50: their warships attack you, their stations refuse you, prices +15 %), **Unfriendly** (-50 to -15: prices +10 %), **Neutral**, **Cordial** (15: prices -2 %, Trusted missions), **Friendly** (40: -5 %, Honoured missions, bounties +10 %) and **Allied** (70: -10 %, Hero missions, bounties +25 %). The station's **Reputation** tab shows where you stand with everyone.

![](shot:station_reputation)
- **Raising it** (slowly - a mission adds 0.1 to 0.4): missions at their stations; trading there (every 10,000 dr bought or sold: +1); hunting Sea Peoples raiders in their space.
- **Losing it**: attacking their ships - the first shot at one costs 2, each one destroyed 8 (their war enemies think a little better of you); shooting down a civilian in another empire's space annoys that empire too. It takes several ships to turn an empire against you, and a bad name fades back toward Neutral by about 1 a minute.
- **Independents**: free ports and ships that answer to no empire. Neutral with everyone and at war with no one - only the Sea Peoples prey on them. A quarter of the civilian ships you meet are independent.
- **Combined invasions and distress calls**: an invasion gathers **two or three fleets** at a staging system on the border, each from a system of its own; when they're all there (or after two minutes) they set out together. A station under attack sends a **distress call**: the nearest idle defence fleets of its owner - and of the owner's **allies** at war with the attacker - within 4 jumps answer it (two at most); allies go home when the danger is over.
- **War missions** (from stations of empires at war, or with an invasion coming): **Protect** a system an invasion is heading for (destroy so many of the invader's warships there), **Strike** an enemy station (take a share of its condition off - it costs you standing with its owner), **Join** one of their fleets (fly within 1,600 of its ships for a minute or more, wherever it goes) or **Raid** an enemy fleet (destroy so many of its ships, wherever it goes).
- **Fleets and invasions**: every empire keeps **war fleets** of 3 to 12 warships. Defence fleets hold its systems (about one for every three) and hurry to a besieged system nearby; at war, an empire gathers **invasion fleets** against the enemy systems on its border (the news tells you). Where fleets of empires at war meet, they fight; an invasion with no defenders left **besieges** the stations of the empires it's at war with - and once the owner has no station left in a system, the system falls to the invader. In the system you're in, the fleets are real ships, and a fleet flies and fights **as one**: on patrol or on its way, its warships keep a **wedge** behind their leader; in a fight they all take **one target** (the leader's, or whichever foe one of them engaged) and spread out in an **arc** round it at their firing distance, the arc swinging round as the leader circles. **Attack one ship and the whole fleet counter-attacks**. You see the invaders go for the stations, and you can join either side (attacking an empire's ships still costs you standing with it). A peace sends invasions home.
- **Damaged stations**: a station worn down below 40 % **burns** - flames and smoke on it - and offers only crisis jobs: **Repairs** (bring materials: machinery, ore, energy cells, electronics - it mends the station, and raises your standing with its owner) and, while it's besieged, **Defend** (destroy so many of the besieger's warships in the system). Stations mend slowly once a siege is over. At 0 a station is **destroyed for good** (the home system's stations can burn but never fall).
- **Who runs the stations**: in every system the empire holding it runs most of the stations. The others are **independent** free ports, an ally's **outpost** (opened with the owner's leave, when they are on good terms and the ally holds a system next door) or a **forward base** of an empire at war with the owner - it wears the system's control down from inside, and with it the system may fall. When a system changes hands, the loser's stations there go to the winner; an outpost of an empire no longer welcome declares itself independent. The galaxy page and the sector map show a station's owner when it isn't the system's.

## quests | Main quest and missions | keywords: Accept mission, Abandon, Accept the main quest, Kilon Alios, quest giver, Reputation
- **The Thread of Ariadne** is the story campaign in 7 chapters. **Kilon Alios** gives it to you on Amnissos, by the landing pad: click him to talk (his portrait shows in the dialogue box), ask about **The signal in the sky**, then **Accept** (or **Not now**); its opening plays there and it starts when you're back in space. Talk to him again later and he tells you where the thread leads now. The station's Main Quests tab shows how far you are; its journal is in the Ship Computer's QUEST tab and the objective shows on the HUD. Its bosses: Asterion's flagship, Talos the bronze guardian, and at the very heart of the Labyrinth **the Minotaur** - the true Asterion, a horned giant crowned in bronze, ringed in gold. He fires bullet-hell patterns of red and gold orbs from the gem on his crest, and every third attack he **lowers his horns and charges** straight at you (his eyes blaze first: sidestep). Defeating him pays 2,500 drachmas, 3 data cores and 5 alien alloy.

![](shot:station_missions)

![](shot:computer_quest)
- **Missions** (each station's Missions tab; eight on offer): up to five at once - Pirate Sweep, Hunt, Courier, Supply Run (deliver trade goods to another station), Salvage Request / Mining Contract (bring salvage or ore here), Survey (fly to an uncharted point, marked on your map). Four tiers - Routine, Trusted, Honoured, Hero - need reputation 0 / 10 / 25 / 50 with the station's empire and pay 1x / 1.5x / 2.2x / 3.2x; the ones you aren't trusted with yet are greyed out and can't be taken. Each finished mission raises your reputation with that empire (+1 / +2 / +3 / +4). **Turn in** salvage and mining jobs for the reward; **Abandon** frees a slot. **Pay** follows how hard a job is: its tier (Routine, Trusted, Honoured, Hero) and how dangerous its kind (a courier run or a survey is safe; supply, salvage and repairs a little risky; bounties, joining a fleet and defence dangerous; hunts, strikes, protecting a system and raiding fleets the most) - from about 500 dr for a Routine courier run to tens of thousands for a Hero-tier fight.

# computer-ch | The Ship Computer
Your ship's information window (Tab).

## computer | The Ship Computer | keywords: Close the Ship Computer, Quest, Inventory, Tech, Repair, Archive
Press **Tab** (or **I**) to open it - always on the **Inventory**; the game goes on while it's open, and it closes by itself if you're attacked. Tabs (keys **1-8**): **Inventory** (cargo, supplies, equipment), **Map** (M), **Galaxy** (G), **Quest** (the story journal), **Tech Tree** (upgrades bought with drachmas and Data Cores), **Repair** (the [Repair Bay](doc:repair-bay)), **Industry** (the [refinery and fabricator](doc:industry)) and **Archive** ([every book](doc:archive): this guide, the tutorial, the encyclopedia - places, people, ships, history; it lists only what you've discovered, and grows as you explore: fly near a ship of a class, up to a station, a planet or an asteroid, hold an item, see gear at an outfitter; the lore unlocks with the main quest - the controls, the versions).

![](shot:computer_inventory)

![](shot:computer_tech)

## repair-bay | The Repair Bay: damaged parts, by hand | keywords: Repair Bay, Scanner, Welder, Soldering iron, Sealant, Calibrator, Forceps, Structure, Thermal, Field, Resonance, Spare, Power, Diagnostic Scanner, Deep Scanner, Fix the ship's parts, Fix the automaton's parts, Surgery, Anatomy, Muscles, Veins, Nerves, Skeleton, Scalpel, Suture, Bone fuser, Clamp, Splicer, Tuner, Nerve block, Incision
Hits that get through to your **hull** (or your automaton's frame on foot) can damage a **part**. Your ship has eight - Sensor Array, Weapon Mounts, Reactor Core, Shield Emitter, Manoeuvring Thrusters, Main Engines, Fuel Lines, Hull Plating; your automaton six - Optic Head, Power Core, Arm Actuators, Heat Sinks, Leg Servos, Chassis Frame - and each one does something: damaged engines lose speed, a damaged emitter weaker shields, damaged fuel lines leak fuel, damaged plating or a damaged frame lets more damage through, damaged legs slow your walking. Some act up as well: damaged **thrusters** jerk the ship off course and set its nose wobbling, damaged **weapon mounts** lose the target now and then and fire wild for a second or two (the Electro and the Bouncer fizzle, a beam swings off), damaged **sensors** scatter your shots. Where a hit lands matters: from behind it finds the engines and fuel lines, from ahead the sensors. The log says what was hit; what's wrong in it you have to find out. **Other ships** suffer the same: hits through to an enemy's hull damage its parts - slower, weaker shields, jerking about, firing wild - and the log tells you what you hit.

The **Repair Bay** is a tab of the Ship Computer and of the Field Computer (**Ship** and **Automaton** at its top). On the left: the schematic and the parts, each with how well it works, the faults found in it (⚠) and **?** where there's damage not yet traced. Click a part to put it on the **operating table**. On the right: its **vitals** - a pulse that races as the part heats up, the temperature, the pressure (leaks lower it), how well it works and its power - the **breaker**, the **tools**, the **scan modes**, your **spare parts** and the faults found here (click one to take the tool it needs).

- **Open it up**: **click a bolt** (anywhere near it, whatever tool you hold) to undo it. Undo **opposite** bolts in turn: two neighbours one after the other strain the casing (it glows red), and a strained casing **warps**: the bolts seize and take a few more turns each. Nothing you do at the table makes a new fault - faults come only from hits to the hull (or the automaton's body).
- **Find the faults**: the **Scanner** - sweep its lens over the part; rest it on a fault and it's marked. Each kind shows in one mode: **Structure** (cracks; wrecked components are plain to see once the casing's off), **Thermal** (leaks, as cold plumes), **Field** (burnt wiring) and **Resonance** (misaligned parts). Your ship's built-in scanner has Structure and Thermal; the **Diagnostic Scanner Mk II** adds Field and Resonance; the **Deep Scanner Mk III** reads through a closed casing (stations sell them with the supplies).
- **Crack**: the **Welder** - hold the button and trace the crack end to end, **slowly**: too fast and the bead doesn't take; resting in one place burns through. Watch the temperature: at its limit the welder **cuts out** and the hot bead cracks back - half the weld to do again.
- **Burnt wiring**: the **Soldering iron** - drag each frayed strand to the terminal of its own colour. **Cut the power first** (the breaker): a live cable **shocks** you and heats the part; the wrong terminal shorts.
- **Leak**: the **Sealant** - hold it on the leak while its gauge is in the **green** (low pressure); at high pressure the sealant is blown away. An open part with a live leak vents and heats up while you work.
- **Misalignment**: the **Calibrator** - drag the **frequency** and **phase** dials up and down until your wave lies on the reference, and hold it there a moment.
- **Wrecked component**: the **Forceps** - click its two clamps open, drag it out, click the empty socket to take a **spare part** of its kind (circuit board, conduit, servo, plate, lens or power cell), **turn** it with the wheel or a right-click until its notch meets the socket's, click to seat it and close the clamps.

Close the casing (click the empty holes) when you're done. Spare parts come from salvaged wrecks and station supplies; a part switched off at its breaker does nothing until you switch it back on.

![](shot:repair_bay)

**The automaton is operated on as a body.** Choose **Automaton** and the table shows its **anatomy**, lying with its head to the left, in **four layers** - the buttons under the tools (where the ship has its scan modes): **1 Muscles** (the muscle bundles and their tendons), **2 Veins** (the heart, the arteries red and the veins blue, the lungs' vessels, the kidneys), **3 Nerves** (the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves out of it to every limb) and **4 Skeleton**. Each of its six parts is a region of the body - the table closes in on it - and its components are structures of one layer at their place on the body: the Arm Actuators are the right biceps and the left forearm's flexors (muscles), the right brachial artery (veins), the right median nerve (nerves) and the left upper arm bone (skeleton); the Power Core is the heart with the aorta, the vena cava, the breastbone and a chest muscle; and so on. Its muscles take a spare **servo**, its vessels a **conduit**, its nerves a **circuit board**, its bones a **plate**.

- **Find the faults**: the **Scanner** shows the faults of the **layer you're looking at** - go through the layers. Your built-in scanner reads the muscles and the veins; the nerves and the skeleton need a **Diagnostic Scanner Mk II**; a **Deep Scanner** shows every layer's faults at once. What is destroyed outright shows to any scanner (a destroyed muscle is plain to see at once).
- **Cut down to it**: the muscles are the surface - worked on directly. A fault deeper (a vessel, a nerve, a bone) is reached through an **incision**: with the **Scalpel**, hold the button and draw the blade along the **dashed line** over it, steadily (too fast and it skips). The wound is held open by retractors and shows the layers beneath, whichever layer you're looking at.
- **Tear** (a muscle, a vessel's wall, a nerve's sheath): the **Suture** - click each mark along the tear to put a stitch there. The same closes an incision (its marks show with the needle in hand); leaving the part closes what you left open.
- **Fracture**: the **Bone fuser** - trace the break end to end, slowly, like a weld; it heats the same way (at the limit it cuts out and half the break cracks back).
- **Bleeding vessel**: the **Clamp** - click the ring on the vessel upstream of the hole: while it holds, the pressure stays down (about 14 seconds - then the tissue needs its blood, and a few seconds before the next). Then the **Sealant**, held on the hole while its gauge is in the green. Without a clamp, only in the lows of the pulse.
- **Burnt nerve**: the **Splicer** - each frayed fibre to the end of its own colour. Numb the part first with the **Nerve block** (the button where the ship has its breaker): a live nerve **shocks**. A numbed part does nothing until the block is lifted. The heart can't be numbed - and has no nerve of its own to splice.
- **Spasm** (in the heart: **arrhythmia**): the **Tuner** - rate and phase onto the reference wave, and held.
- **Destroyed** structure: the **Forceps** - click its two ties undone, drag the dead piece out, click the wound to take a spare as a **graft**, turn it (wheel / right-click) until it lies the way the tissue runs, click to graft it, then click the two ties.

![](shot:surgery)

## industry | Industry: refinery, fabricator, upgrade kits | keywords: Industry, Refinery, Fabricator, Refine, Make, Upgrade Kit, Fit, Fragments
The Ship Computer's **INDUSTRY** tab: your ship's own industry, working on in the background while you fly (a queue on the right - ✕ stops a job and gives back what wasn't used).

- **Refinery** (equipment, outfitters' SYSTEMS; the cargo bay): turns the **fragments** your mining laser cuts into their minerals, a unit each (1.2 s a unit; the reactor's refinery upgrade makes it faster) - worth two and a half times as much. Rubble gives scrap and now and then a mineral.
- **Fabricator** (equipment; the hull): makes things from minerals and goods - over thirty **recipes** in six groups: **materials** (bronze ingots, girders, hull plates, rivets, glass, power cables, coolant, fuel, water), **components** (bearings, circuit boards, capacitor banks, processors, servos, optic fibre, tools, reactor coils), **spare parts** for the Repair Bay, **supplies** (missiles, repair kits), small **weapons** (extra-small pulse and plasma cannons, a missile launcher) and **Upgrade Kits**. Each card shows what it takes (what you have of each), how long and what it sells for: the markets buy the materials and components - mining, refining and making things is a living.
- **Kits** - fit a component upgrade yourself: a **Mk I** kit raises a stat from level 0 or 1, a **Mk II** from 2 or 3, a **Mk III** from 4 to the top (the same stats as a station's UPGRADES).

![](shot:industry)

## sector-map | The sector map | keywords: Map, Whole sector, Centre on your ship
The map of the system you're in: stations, planets, ships, asteroids and your objective. **Trade** (the cart button, or **T**) shows the best trade runs from this system's stations you've charted: green arrows to another station here, or to the gate on the way to a station up to two jumps away (named on the tag), with the good to carry and the profit a unit. Click to set a course; **Shift + click** adds a **waypoint** to it - the ship flies through them in order (numbered on the map) without stopping, and stops at the last; **Shift + drag** a waypoint (the cursor turns to a move cross over one) to move it - let go on a station, planet or gate and it snaps to it; a plain click starts a new course, attacking something drops it. The wheel zooms (a click of the middle button puts the zoom back - in every view that zooms), dragging pans; **Whole sector** shows everything you've found, **Centre on your ship** finds you. On planets built in levels the map and minimap show the **elevation**: higher ground lighter, lower ground darker, each level's edge outlined where the ground drops, ramps marked pale. **Fog of war**: only what your sensors have swept (about 2,800 units round your ship, wherever you've flown) shows - the rest of the system is dark, its stations, planets and gates hidden until you get near them; ships show only within sensor range. Your objective always shows. The radar's rim arrows point only at stations and gates you've found. What you've explored is remembered, system by system. **Navigation beacons**: every system has one beside its star - right-click it (from within 1.6k) and your ship **scans** it - 6 seconds: a beam from your ship, a scan line sweeping the beacon, a ring filling round it, SCANNING and how far; fly out of range and the scan is lost - and then the whole system is **charted** for good: the fog lifts from all of it, and every planet, moon, station and jump gate shows on the map and the radar (its stations count as seen for trade runs, its planets go into the Encyclopedia). Before that it's just the beacon, turning slowly, reading RIGHT-CLICK TO SCAN; once it has charted the system it comes alive, green - a glowing, pulsating ring, and scanning waves leaving it in every direction, each trailing holographic nebula gas that lingers and fades - and reads CHARTED. It shows on the map and the radar too (amber, then green), once you've seen where it stands.

![](shot:nav_beacon)



![](shot:computer_map)

## nav-reports | Navigation reports | keywords: nav beacon, report, sell, chart
Scan a system's **navigation beacon** (right-click it, then stay within 1.6k for 6 seconds) and it gives you a **navigation report** of the system as it is right now - it doesn't lift the fog (your sensors still have to find things on the map), it tells you what's there. The report opens at once: the system's **stations** (and who holds each), its **jump gates** (and where they lead), its **planets and moons** (the landable ones in green), the **ships** about - **hostile** ones by who they are (pirates, an empire at war with you), **friendly and neutral** ones by empire, and all of them by trade (traders, miners, patrols...) - any **monsters**, and how many asteroids, wrecks and signals there are. Right-click the beacon again while you're still in the system to see it again (✕ or Esc closes it).

A copy goes into your hold - **one a visit**: leave the system and come back for another. **Stations in other systems buy reports** (Sell tab): the further the report's system is from theirs, the more they pay - 60 drachmas, plus 70 for every jump between the two systems and 10 for each of its stations. In its own system a report is worthless. Hover a report in your hold for its summary.

![](shot:nav_report)

## galaxy | The galaxy | keywords: Galaxy, Plot route, Clear route
**Galaxy space** - **New Hellas** - reached only through this map. Fifty-eight systems linked by **jump gates**. Each has an owner - the **Minoan Thalassocracy**, the **Athenian League**, the **Spartan Hegemony**, the **Mycenaean Kingdoms**, the **Ionian League**, the **Cycladic Isles** (each holding 8 to 10 systems round its heartland) - or the Sea Peoples (five dens). The **Cycladic Isles** are the oldest seafarers of the Aegean: white marble and black obsidian ships and stations, folded-arm figurines, spirals and longboats; friends of the Minoans, wary of the mainland. Empires go to war and make peace; border systems change hands. Click a system and **Plot route**: the HUD points you to each gate in turn. **Shift + click** a system to add it to the end of the route (a waypoint): the route goes on from there, so you can go round several systems in one trip. **Trade routes** (the cart button, or **T**) turns on the trade layer: the best runs between systems (buy at a station, sell at one up to two jumps away - one run a pair of systems, the ten best) as green arrows along the gate lanes, labelled with the good and the profit a unit, the best brightest; pick one good or all of them. The right column lists them; click one to plot a route to where you buy. They follow the prices as they move. Fly into a gate to jump. Each gate is a great armoured ring around a turning blue vortex, glowing faintly in the colour of the empire that owns the system it leads to; a ring of light bursts out of it as you go through, and again from the gate you come out of.

![](shot:computer_galaxy)
- **Planets and moons**: every system beyond Knossos has 1 to 12 planets, each one of the four kinds you know from home - **volcanic** worlds (like Akrotiri) close to the star, **ocean** worlds (like Amnissos) further out, **ice** worlds (like Ida) and **gas giants** (like Dikte) at the edge. Some have **moons** - grey, cratered little worlds like Kamares, named after their planet (Gournia I, Gournia II...); gas giants can have up to three. You can land on every one of them: each has its kind's land, beasts and climate (the heat of a volcanic world, the ice underfoot), but its own map and name. The galaxy page counts a system's planets and moons; on the system map a moon's name shows once you zoom in.

# planets-ch | Planets
Walking on Amnissos, Kamares and Ida.

## planets | On the surface | keywords: Stairs, Part
Land with the **land** button over a planet. Planets are big - 440 x 440 tiles, a few minutes to cross on foot - with Minoan villages scattered across them: a palace, warehouse and temple by your landing pad, and more villages out in the wilds. The world appears around you as you go (the minimap at the top right shows the land near you).

![](shot:surface_walk)
- You walk the surface as an armoured **android** with a rifle (it turns to face the way you walk - walking when it's slow, running at its full pace). To fight an enemy, **click it** (left or right button - the cursor turns to a crosshair over one), or press **F** for the nearest: you close in if it's out of range, shoulder the rifle and fire until it falls - or, in a martial style, run up and fight it hand to hand (see [Skills](doc:skills)). Clicking the ground (or it getting away) ends the fight. **Click** to walk, or hold the button to keep walking toward the cursor. The land is built like the limestone hills of Greece: **ledges** of grass and woodland one above another, with limestone **cliffs** where a ledge ends and **ramps** between them - the ways up and down (villages, the landing site and the portals stand on level ground). Amnissos is drawn from its own tile set - Greek ground in the style of 1980s anime: olive groves, cypresses, holm oaks and pines, oleander and lavender, boulders and the odd fallen column, sandy beaches and the Aegean blue sea. Ida and its neighbour moon Kamares are drawn from an ice tile set: snowfields and blue-ice cliffs, crystal clusters, snowy pines and dead trees, and frozen Greek ruins; Ida's crevasse winds across it like a frozen river. Cliffs, crags, water and crevasses block the way - exactly where they're drawn; paths go around them, or up the nearest slope (and around the scree and boulders at a crag's foot). Each planet has one body of water rather than pools everywhere: Amnissos a coastline with a few islets offshore, Ida one long crevasse winding across it with ice bridges over it; other worlds a lake or a river with fords.
- **Buildings** - walk in through their sliding doors. Palaces have several rooms; bigger buildings have an **upper floor**: click the **stairs** to climb (or simply click a spot upstairs - the path takes the stairs), and click the stairwell upstairs to come down.
- **Minoan citizens** - guards with laser rifles patrol and shoot anything hostile, and so do the **Minoan androids**: machines of ceramic and bronze built in a triceratops's image, with a frill painted in red spirals and glowing cyan eyes, named for the automata of the Cretan myths, such as Talos. They are tougher than flesh and armed three ways: a **laser rifle** (bursts of bolts), a **laser bow** (one hard-hitting arrow at a time, from further off) or a **labrys**, the Minoan double axe (it strides up to a foe and cleaves it). Click one to hear what they say (the translation is in the event log).
- **Kilon Alios** - a hooded wanderer in a long coat, standing by the landing pad on Amnissos (and turning to watch you come): the maintainer of this world, serving **Ephestos**, god of science and technology. Click him to talk: after his greeting you can ask him **who he is**, **who you are** (an automaton built by Ephestos himself, to improve and gather knowledge), **where you are** (New Hellas and its empires, each with its strengths and weaknesses), **what your mission is** and **what you should become** - the choice is yours. He also gives you the main quest (**The signal in the sky**). The yellow triangle over his head shows while he has it to give. He stands by the landing pad of **every** world: there he greets you as one of its people and tells of them - who they are, their gods, their great deeds - and, everywhere, the story of **New Hellas** (how it began, who built the gates, why the empires quarrel, where the gods are now, the Atrapos sector).
- **The empires' stories** - besides the Minoans' Thread of Ariadne, each great empire has its own main quest, told by Kilon Alios as the old singers told theirs. Dock at its capital to begin: **The Olive and the Owl** (Athenai Stoa), **With Your Shield or On It** (Sparta Barracks), **The Mask of Gold** (Mykenai Forge), **The First Principle** (Miletos Agora), **The Wandering Isle** (Delos Circle). Each runs across several systems - deliveries, battles, oracles and a monster of its own myths - and its objective shows under the minimap. Enemies a story sends to another system wait there for you, and come back if you leave before they're beaten.
- **The empires' worlds** - a planet's buildings follow the people who hold its system: Athenian marble and blue, Spartan red and bronze, Mycenaean stone and gold, Ionian lapis and gold, Cycladic whitewash - each with pieces of its own (Athena's owl and painted kraters, racks of lambda shields, the Lion Gate relief, Ionic columns and star globes, folded-arm marble figures).
- **Pirates** - bands of pirate raiders (evil androids in tattered coats; red on the minimap) roam every planet, and prowl near the villages. They shoot you and the citizens on sight - never each other - and the guards, archers and androids shoot back. Laser bolts and arrows are fast and home in on their target: you can't outrun or dodge them - fight back, or get out of range before they fire. Up close they sling the rifle and fight **hand to hand** - jabs, hooks, kicks, a sweep - and now and then block a blow of yours; one in three is a **brawler** who charges you instead of shooting. Fight them yourself: click one (or press F). Shoot a pirate and it fights back - if you fire from beyond its reach it comes after you - but a badly hurt pirate lowers its rifle and runs for it (you're faster: chase it down, or let it go). A fallen pirate drops a glowing chest: walk over it for drachmas and, often, some cargo (scrap, energy cells, weapons, data cores...). You hear them before you see them: their footsteps, the whir of a rifle coming up and the zap of its bolts, a robotic grunt when hit, a growled taunt (click one), an alarm when one runs, and the crash when one falls. The volumes are in the title screen's Settings.
- **What you carry** - on a planet everything you pick up (loot, ore, salvage, Cybernetic Matter, medicine...) goes to **you**: you carry **12 slots**, up to **100** of an item in each (shown next to your drachmas, and in the Field Computer). When they're full, loot stays where it lies and chests won't open. **Click your ship** for the transfer screen: what you carry beside the ship's hold - click a stack to move it across (up to 100 at a time), or **drag** it into a slot on the other side or to another slot on its own side - and **Take off**. What you carry stays with you when you take off (in the Ship Computer's inventory, click a stack to put it in the hold).
- **Health and shield** - the gauge under the planet's panel: the automaton's outline filled with red liquid as high as its health is, inside a blue ring filled as high as its **shield** is (hover the ring for the numbers). Pirates' bolts hit the shield first - what it soaks never reaches you or your parts - and it recharges quickly once you're 3 seconds out of the fight; health comes back once you're out of the fight for a few seconds.
